title: Measuring economic activity from outer space

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Looking down from orbit hundreds of kilometers above the sunlit surface of the Earth, the signposts of civilization are clearly visible. The patterns of farmland; the lines of roads and railways; Egypt's Great Pyramid and China's Great Wall – all are easily seen. But passing into night, the signs of humanity fade save for one: light from artificial sources like street lamps and domestic lighting. Back in 1962, when John Glenn orbited the Earth, he demonstrated that lights at night made it possible for human activity to be traced from space. Passing over western Australia, he reported seeing a very bright light; the citizens of Perth had turned on all their lights as a signal to him when they knew he would be flying overhead. Since then, satellite imagery of night-time lights has been used with some success to measure developments on our planet. Static snapshots can reveal stark contrasts, like the brightly glowing lights of prosperous cities on Saudi Arabia's eastern coast and the darkness of the desert further inland. Gradual developments can be discerned, too, like the economic growth of megacities such as Tokyo and Mumbai. All such observations to date have been quite crude, since most of the data comes from one source, the US Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP), an ageing network of satellites which can only produce low resolution snapshots.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: But new analytical techniques are now improving the way we measure economic activity from space. American economists J Vernon Henderson and David Weil recently analyzed over a decade's worth of global night-light data from DMSP. Their research shows a link between changes in a country's Gross Domestic Product* (GDP) and the intensity of its electric lighting, both domestic and commercial: on average, as a country's GDP increases, its night-time light emission becomes more intense. The work is particularly promising for measuring growth in the developing world, where reliable statistics are hard to get.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Henderson and his colleagues also used the DMSP data to examine economic activity on sub-national scales, investigating the relationship of African cities to nearby agricultural regions. They found that years of crop-boosting high rainfall in a city's hinterlands significantly correlated with increased growth and development in the urban center, as measured by artificial lighting intensity. It is clear that hinterlands are relevant to the growth and development of cities. Henderson says, 'Farmers require a bunch of products, they demand services – this makes a lot of difference to a nearby city.'

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Of course, there are dangers in using night-time lights as an indicator for economic growth. The DMSP satellites have limited capabilities to measure light intensity, and their images are not well defined. Chris Elvidge leads a team that removes contaminating natural phenomena like moonlight, lightning, and forest fires from the images, but he says that human choices of how buildings and streets are lit, and even which variety of light bulbs are used, all alter the patterns and intensity of light, adding uncertainty to any conclusions.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Still, even uncertain data seems better than none at all. Elvidge and his team have used night-time DMSP data to detect gas flares, the deliberate burning of excess natural gas left over from petroleum production, which may account for as much as 2% of all the carbon released into the atmosphere each year by human activity. The satellite data proved that some countries were grossly under-reporting their gas flaring. Such information will become increasingly important if global schemes are negotiated for reducing levels of carbon released.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: According to Paul Sutton, a geographer and collaborator with the DMSP team, measuring artificial lighting may become one of the best ways for estimating how technology affects humanity's ecological footprint on Earth. Sutton is suggesting to NASA** that it should develop and launch a Nightsat, a state-of-the-art satellite devoted solely to gathering high resolution, full-color data on nocturnal lights across the globe. Sutton says, 'As the world's population increases, our ability to know what all the human beings are doing on this planet is getting increasingly vague, and a Nightsat mission is one way to get objective global coverage of what's going on. Its data could help quantify energy usage, economic activity, and more.'

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: 'This all goes back to the idea of "carrying capacity",' Sutton adds, and explains the concept in the following way: 'You can only put so many goldfish in a tank before they're killed by their own waste, and you can only raise so many cattle on a given area of land.' Humans are in a unique position, because Earth's carrying capacity for us depends on how we choose to live and to use technology. But our influence on Earth's carrying capacity is often unpredictable and difficult to discern. Sometimes our choices will increase the impact we have on the environments we live in; sometimes they will decrease the consequences. But, Sutton says, night-time satellite imagery seems a good way to go about minimizing the damage.

content: Paul Sutton explains the idea of carrying capacity by referring to the number of {{24}} that will survive in a container and also the number of {{25}} that can be kept on a particular piece of land.
